title: Father calls for apology after son target of racist taunts at Kitchener, Ont., hockey tournament
summary: The father of a 16-year-old hockey player says he wants a public apology and cultural-competency training for the league after his son was the target of racist taunts at a tournament in Kitchener,…

image.caption: Ryder Doxtator of the Brantford 99ers and his dad Aaron Doxtator at Little NHL. (Submitted by Aaron Doxtator)

blocks.text: Indigenous

The father of a 16-year-old hockey player says he wants a public apology and cultural-competency training for the league after his son was the target of racist taunts at a tournament in Kitchener, Ont., on Nov. 8.
Kitchener Minor Hockey Association and ALLIANCE Hockey investigating
In a video provided to CBC Indigenous, a player on the Kitchener Jr. Rangers can be heard telling Brantford 99ers player Ryder Doxtator "Go back to the rez."

Aaron Doxtator, Ryder's father, from Oneida Nation of the Thames, was at his son's game Nov. 8. He said his son told him that he'd also been called a "dirty Indian" by the same player. Although Aaron Doxtator said he was unable to hear it from the stands, he said other players and staff on Ryder's team and parents told him they also heard the slur.
As a former athlete in hockey and lacrosse who experienced this type of racism throughout his playing career, Aaron Doxtator said he can't believe it's still happening.
Ryder Doxtator of the Brantford 99ers was told to 'go back to the rez' by a player on the Kitchener Jr. Rangers. (Submitted by Aaron Doxtator)

"It's always the same words, 'Go back to where you came from. Go back to the rez, you dirty Indian, or go back to your teepees.' Those are all different words I've heard growing up … My older son, happened to him all the way up," Aaron Doxtator said.
"You just get a gross feeling in your stomach when you hear those words."
He said despite being proud of his home, "They're making you feel like you're lower, 'Get out of here. You know you don't belong here.'"

Doxtator said there was a brawl just after Ryder scored a goal with one minute left in the game. The referees broke it up and Ryder was put in the penalty box along with two teammates and three Kitchener Jr. Rangers players.
Doxtator said they were arguing back and forth and a Brantford 99ers trainer went over to the box "to try to defuse the situation and tell our player to calm down."
He said she and a couple of the other parents heard the Kitchener players saying 'go back to the rez' and 'go back to where you came from.'
He was told by officials that the video was under review.
Doxtator said this isn't the first time his son's dealt with racist taunts from opponents.
"It angered him because he's heard that before and it's discriminatory … We should be equal with people," he said.
He said he's lodged formal complaints with leagues before, but they just get "brushed under the rug" and "nothing comes of it."
2 pending investigations into incident
The Kitchener Minor Hockey Association (KMHA) said it received several emails regarding the incident and there are two investigations looking into the incident.

Roland Cyr, general manager for KMHA, said in an emailed statement to CBC Indigenous that KMHA "is aware of allegations involving the use of a racial slur during a game conducted under the jurisdiction of the association."

The statement continued that KMHA is also aware that the matter was reported to the on-ice officials during the game, who documented the allegations and submitted the report to the Minor Hockey Alliance of Ontario (ALLIANCE Hockey) for review.
The statement said KMHA takes the allegations seriously "and is committed to ensuring a safe, respectful, and inclusive environment for all participants in our sport."
It said in accordance with its policies, KMHA will be undertaking a review of the incident and ALLIANCE Hockey, the governing body for both teams, will conduct its own investigation.
Brantford 99ers general manager Kevin Murray declined to comment as the investigation is ongoing.
ALLIANCE Hockey said in an emailed statement it is aware “of an alleged incident that occurred on Nov. 8 at the Kitchener Blueline Tournament" and is taking it seriously.
Previously in 2022, one of KMHA's U-13 Kitchener Lady Rangers players used a racial slur against an opponent and the team had to issue an apology and take part in diversity training.
Racial slurs pop out as they're 'still part of their lexicon,' says academic
Janelle Joseph, Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Racial Justice, Health and Sport at Brock University in St. Catharines, Ont., said incidents like this are sad but not surprising.
Joseph said there's been a lot of work around racial and gender justice in hockey which "continues to be run predominantly by that white majority."
"We are in the midst of a culture shift, but we're not on the other side of it," she said.
Joseph said players understand there are phrases they shouldn't say, "but if it's still part of their lexicon … when they get into the heat of a conflict, it spurts out."

Janelle Joseph is a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Racial Justice, Health and Sport at Brock University and associate professor. She's also the founder and director of Canada's first research laboratory devoted to issues of race and movement cultures, the Indigeneity, Diaspora, Equity and Anti-racism in Sport (IDEAS) Research Lab. (Submitted by Janelle Joseph)

"That means that it was just always there. They were learning ways to cover it up or ways to communicate that would be more socially acceptable. But the anti-Indigenous racism, anti-Black racism, anti-immigrant and xenophobia is underlying in many, many of our communities."
Beyond superficial anti-racism training, Joseph said all teams would benefit from open dialogue about history and "what those expressions mean."
"When someone says 'go back to the rez,' what are they really saying there?" she said.
"I think we need to surface those kinds of conversations across every locker room, every team, so that we can start to make racism not something that happens over there, with those other people."
She said then we can start to see how some of those ideologies and understandings about who belongs and who doesn't are part of the dominant culture.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Candace Maracle is Kanien'kehá:ka, Wolf Clan from Tyendinaga Mohawk Territory. She has a master’s degree in journalism from Toronto Metropolitan University. Her latest short film, Tsi ní:yoht yonkwayentá:’on ne óhses (How We Got Maple Syrup) is completely in the Kanien’kéha language.
